metadata.name: AI Cultural Mappings
metadata.description: Concept-level cultural mappings across English, Tamil, and Japanese — how each culture/language expresses the same underlying social concept, with notes on divergence.
metadata.note: Curated starter set of verified concept mappings, meant to be extended incrementally rather than mass-generated.

mappings.description: How each culture/language emphatically agrees with a statement.

english.cultural_note: Casual, Gen Z-coded emphatic agreement; 'no cap' signals total sincerity.

tamil.cultural_note: 'Definitely/certainly' — used with emphatic tone for strong agreement in daily speech.

japanese.expression: マジで (maji de) / ほんとに (honto ni)
japanese.cultural_note: Emphatic confirmation, common across all ages, softer in tone than English slang equivalents.

mappings.cross_cultural_note: English slang for agreement skews youth/internet-coded; Tamil and Japanese equivalents are used more broadly across age groups without feeling like 'slang'.

mappings.description: The ability to sense group mood and adjust behavior accordingly.

english.cultural_note: Used as a corrective/critical phrase when someone misjudges the mood.

tamil.cultural_note: Situational awareness is valued but not codified as a distinct named social skill the way it is in Japan.

japanese.cultural_note: A foundational, deeply codified social value in Japan; failing at it earns the label 'KY' (kuuki yomenai), a real social criticism.

mappings.cross_cultural_note: Japan uniquely elevates this into a named, teachable social competency; English and Tamil treat it as common sense rather than a distinct skill.

mappings.description: How casual/respectful address terms function differently across cultures.

english.cultural_note: Gender-informal address terms used loosely for friends, rarely carry hierarchy implications.

tamil.expression: அண்ணா (anna) for men, அக்கா (akka) for women
tamil.cultural_note: Literally 'older brother/sister' — used even for strangers to show respect and warmth, reflecting Tamil culture's emphasis on familial framing of social relationships.

japanese.cultural_note: Honorific suffixes are mandatory in most contexts; dropping them (yobisute) signals deep closeness or, if used wrongly, rudeness.

mappings.cross_cultural_note: Tamil and Japanese both encode social hierarchy/relationship into address terms far more than English does; Tamil does so via kinship terms, Japanese via honorific suffixes.

mappings.description: Playful mockery as a marker of closeness rather than hostility.

english.cultural_note: Friendly insult exchange, common in youth and online meme culture.

tamil.cultural_note: Central to Tamil friend-group banter; often loud and public, seen as a sign of comfort and affection.

japanese.cultural_note: Root of Japanese 'manzai' comedy duo dynamics (boke/tsukkomi); playful teasing is a structured comedic and social ritual.

mappings.cross_cultural_note: All three cultures use teasing as bonding, but Japan has formalized it into comedic performance tradition more than the other two.

mappings.description: Softened or indirect ways to express dissatisfaction.

english.cultural_note: Flat or lukewarm tone signals dissatisfaction without direct criticism.

tamil.cultural_note: 'Not quite right' — moderately direct, though softened compared to outright criticism.

japanese.cultural_note: Culturally essential indirectness; Japanese social norms strongly favor avoiding direct negative statements, so 'bimyou' is a key face-saving tool.

mappings.cross_cultural_note: Japanese indirectness here is a deep cultural norm (avoiding direct 'no'), while English/Tamil versions are more casual stylistic choices.

mappings.description: Words used to express something is amazing/extreme, often with flexible or even opposite meanings depending on tone.

english.cultural_note: Youth slang for extreme positive excitement, tone rarely flips negative.

tamil.cultural_note: Intensifier from 'pure/red', now used broadly for 'very/really' or standalone for 'awesome'.

japanese.cultural_note: Originally 'dangerous'; now context-flexible for both amazing and terrible, tone entirely carries the meaning.

mappings.cross_cultural_note: 'Yabai' is unusually flexible even for slang — it can mean the opposite of itself depending on delivery, more so than the English or Tamil equivalents.

mappings.description: Terms for one's favorite celebrity/character and the culture of active fan support.

english.cultural_note: 'Stan' (from an Eminem song) means an obsessive fan; 'bias' is borrowed fandom slang for a favorite member of a group.

tamil.cultural_note: Tamil fan culture centers heavily on cinema stars, with devotion sometimes reaching quasi-religious levels (cutouts, temples for actors).

japanese.cultural_note: Core concept in idol/anime fan culture; 'oshi-katsu' (推し活, supporting one's oshi) is a recognized lifestyle and consumer category.

mappings.cross_cultural_note: All three show fandom as an important cultural institution, but the object of fandom differs: idols/characters (Japan), film stars (Tamil), and more decentralized figures (English-speaking internet).

mappings.description: Expressions describing an unconditionally loyal friend.

english.cultural_note: Originally biker/hip-hop culture, now mainstream for describing ultimate loyalty.

tamil.cultural_note: 'Life-friend' — reflects Tamil culture's framing of deep friendship in near-familial terms.

japanese.cultural_note: Classical Chinese-origin idiom retained in Japanese, literally 'a friend one would die for'; more literary/formal than everyday slang.

mappings.cross_cultural_note: English and Tamil versions are used in everyday casual speech; the Japanese equivalent is more literary, with 親友 (shin'yuu, 'true friend') used as the everyday casual version.

mappings.description: Informal request or act of sharing juicy personal information.

english.cultural_note: From Black and queer ballroom culture ('T' for Truth), now mainstream internet slang.

tamil.cultural_note: Straightforward 'tell me the news' — gossip culture is strong but lacks a distinct poetic slang phrase like 'spill the tea'.

japanese.expression: ゴシップを話す (goshippu wo hanasu) / 噂話 (uwasabanashi)
japanese.cultural_note: 'Uwasabanashi' (rumor talk) is the traditional term; gossip is culturally viewed with more caution given emphasis on group harmony.

mappings.cross_cultural_note: English slang around gossip is playful and colorful; Japanese framing carries more social caution due to harmony-focused norms.

mappings.description: Displaying wealth, success, or dominance, often ostentatiously.

english.cultural_note: Hip-hop-derived, now mainstream for boasting about possessions/achievements.

tamil.cultural_note: 'Showing off' or 'putting on style' — used both playfully among friends and critically for real pretension.

japanese.expression: マウントを取る (maunto wo toru)
japanese.cultural_note: Borrowed from wrestling ('mount'); describes asserting status/dominance, often viewed critically since overt boasting clashes with modesty norms.

mappings.cross_cultural_note: Japan's modesty-valuing norms make 'flexing' more socially frowned upon than in English or Tamil youth culture, where it can be playful self-promotion.
